title: 1 Chronicles 22:1–16
context: David declares the threshing floor the site of the LORD’s house and gathers workers, stone, iron, bronze, and cedar. He charges Solomon, the man of peace, to build what David, a man of war, was not permitted to build, recalling the promise of 2 Samuel 7 and urging him to keep the law. Chronicles alone describes these preparations in such detail; 2 Chronicles 3:1 later identifies the place as Mount Moriah. The very large amounts in 22:14 are discussed by interpreters in different ways.

verses.text: Then David said, “This is the house of the LORD God, and this is the altar of burnt offering for Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: David declares, This is the house of the LORD God, and this is the altar of burnt offering for Israel. Arminian readers see the place of judgment becoming the place of worship, a sign that God’s mercy has the last word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s choice of the site confirmed by the fire of 21:26. 2 Chronicles 3:1 later identifies the place as Mount Moriah; whether this is the Moriah of Genesis 22 is commonly held but debated by interpreters.

verses.text: David gave orders to gather together the foreigners who were in the land of Israel; and he set masons to cut dressed stones to build God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: David gathers the foreigners in the land and sets masons to cut stone. Arminian readers note that people from outside Israel take part in preparing God’s house, a small sign of a wider purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the use of foreign laborers reappears under Solomon (2 Chronicles 2:17). The careful preparation reflects the seriousness with which David approaches the work.

verses.text: David prepared iron in abundance for the nails for the doors of the gates and for the couplings, and bronze in abundance without weight,
verses.arminianNotes: David prepares iron for nails and couplings and bronze beyond weighing. Arminian readers see a king who, though not permitted to build, gives himself fully to making the work possible for another.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the abundance a heart moved to honor God beyond calculation. The materials are described as too much to weigh, a way of stressing generosity rather than recording exact amounts.

verses.text: and cedar trees without number, for the Sidonians and the people of Tyre brought cedar trees in abundance to David.
verses.arminianNotes: Cedar trees without number come from the Sidonians and the people of Tyre. Arminian readers note that neighboring peoples contribute to the work, as Hiram of Tyre had already supplied David’s house (1 Chronicles 14:1).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Tyre and Sidon will again supply timber under Solomon (2 Chronicles 2:8-16). God’s purposes draw in resources from beyond Israel’s borders.

verses.text: David said, “Solomon my son is young and tender, and the house that is to be built for the LORD must be exceedingly magnificent, of fame and of glory throughout all countries. I will therefore make preparation for it.” So David prepared abundantly before his death.
verses.arminianNotes: David says Solomon is young and tender and that the house must be exceedingly magnificent. Arminian readers see a father’s practical love, preparing what his son could not yet gather alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the house is to be of fame and of glory throughout all countries, pointing beyond Israel to the nations. David’s preparation serves God’s glory, not only his son’s convenience.

verses.text: Then he called for Solomon his son, and commanded him to build a house for the LORD, the God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: David calls Solomon and commands him to build a house for the LORD. Arminian readers see a solemn handing on of responsibility, in which Solomon is called to carry out a task he must freely embrace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the commission as part of the promise God gave in 2 Samuel 7. The charge is personal, yet it rests on God’s prior word about David’s son.

verses.text: David said to Solomon his son, “As for me, it was in my heart to build a house to the name of the LORD my God.
verses.arminianNotes: David says it was in his heart to build a house to the name of the LORD. Arminian readers see godly desire honored even when God redirects it, as David’s intention was good though its fulfillment belonged to another.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David’s wish appears in 2 Samuel 7:2 and 1 Chronicles 17:1. God accepts the desire while overruling the plan, a pattern both traditions recognize.

verses.text: But the LORD’s word came to me, saying, ‘You have shed blood abundantly and have made great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed much blood on the earth in my sight.
verses.arminianNotes: God said David could not build because he had shed much blood and made great wars. Arminian readers note that the reason is stated more directly here than in 2 Samuel 7, and they read it as a matter of fitness for the task rather than condemnation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that 1 Kings 5:3 links the delay to the wars that surrounded David, while Chronicles speaks of the blood he shed (compare 1 Chronicles 28:3). Both accounts are named without forcing one into the other.

verses.text: Behold, a son shall be born to you, who shall be a man of peace. I will give him rest from all his enemies all around; for his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quietness to Israel in his days.
verses.arminianNotes: A son will be born who will be a man of peace, and God will give him rest. Arminian readers see God preparing a season of peace for the work of building, so that worship can flourish without the distraction of war.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the name Solomon is commonly connected with the Hebrew word for peace, which the verse itself suggests. The rest promised is God’s gift, not Solomon’s achievement.

verses.text: He shall build a house for my name; and he will be my son, and I will be his father; and I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever.’
verses.arminianNotes: He shall build a house for my name; and he will be my son, and I will be his father. Arminian readers see the promise of 2 Samuel 7:13-14 restated, with Solomon called to live faithfully within the covenant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Davidic covenant as shared ground, as the earlier notes on 2 Samuel 7 treat it. Hebrews 1:5 applies the words I will be his father to Christ, which many Christians read as their fullest fulfillment.

verses.text: Now, my son, may the LORD be with you and prosper you, and build the house of the LORD your God, as he has spoken concerning you.
verses.arminianNotes: David prays that the LORD will be with Solomon and prosper him. Arminian readers see a father’s blessing that depends on God’s presence while still calling the son to faithful work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David grounding the task in God’s promise, as he has spoken concerning you. The work will succeed because God has spoken, a confidence that shapes the whole charge.

verses.text: May the LORD give you discretion and understanding, and put you in charge of Israel, so that you may keep the law of the LORD your God.
verses.arminianNotes: David asks God to give Solomon discretion and understanding so he may keep the law. Arminian readers note that wisdom is sought as a gift and then put to use in obedience, a partnership of grace and response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wisdom as God’s gift, enabling obedience to his law and fitting Solomon to rule. The request anticipates Solomon’s own prayer for wisdom (2 Chronicles 1:10).

verses.text: Then you will prosper, if you observe to do the statutes and the ordinances which the LORD gave Moses concerning Israel. Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid and don’t be dismayed.
verses.arminianNotes: You will prosper if you observe the statutes. Be strong and courageous. Arminian readers see a genuine condition attached to the promise, calling Solomon to faithfulness that he must choose day by day.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear an echo of the charge to Joshua (Joshua 1:6-9). The promise and the command belong together, and how the traditions read such conditions is treated in the Leviticus 26:3 box.

verses.text: Now, behold, in my affliction I have prepared for the LORD’s house one hundred thousand talents of gold, one million talents of silver, and bronze and iron without weight; for it is in abundance. I have also prepared timber and stone; and you may add to them.
verses.arminianNotes: In his affliction David prepared one hundred thousand talents of gold and one million talents of silver. Arminian readers see sacrificial giving from a king who prepared through hardship for a house he would never see.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the amounts are enormous, and interpreters discuss them in different ways, some reading them as round or hyperbolic figures and others as possibly affected in transmission. The point both traditions draw is lavish provision for God’s house.

verses.text: There are also workmen with you in abundance—cutters and workers of stone and timber, and all kinds of men who are skillful in every kind of work;
verses.arminianNotes: Workmen are available in abundance, skilled in every kind of work. Arminian readers see human skill as something to be offered to God, valued and used in the service of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God supplying not only materials but people with the gifts the work requires, recalling the skilled workers of the tabernacle (Exodus 31:1-6).

verses.text: of the gold, the silver, the bronze, and the iron, there is no number. Arise and be doing, and may the LORD be with you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arise and be doing, and may the LORD be with you. Arminian readers see the charge to act, trusting that God’s presence will accompany faithful effort.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the command to work resting on the prayer for God’s presence. Preparation is complete; now the son must act, depending on the God who promised.
